title: Auger Electron Spectroscopy; A Complementary Technique to Scanning Electron Microscopy
content: Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES), named after French physicist Pierre Victor Auger who observed these radiationless transitions in 1923 and detailed these observations in 1925, but was also independently discovered by Austrian-born physicist Lise Meitner in 1923 [1], is a technique for analyzing the element(s) constituting a sample surface, its composition, and chemical bonding state by irradiating the sample surface with a focused electron beam and measuring the kinetic energy of the Auger electrons emitted from the first 2-10 atomic layers [2-4] with a surface layer defined as generally being up to three atomic layers thick (∼1 nm), depending upon the material [5,6]. Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES) is one of the main types of surface analysis, with the 3 main types of surface analysis being Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES), Time of Flight -Secondary Ion Mass Spectroscopy (TOF-SIMS), and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) [7-9]. Of these 3 main surface science techniques, Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES) offers the highest spatial resolution, with a laterally spatial resolution of ≥10 nm [8-10].
